title: What are law firms actually using AI for?
description: Where AI pays first in a mid-size law firm, which ethics and court rules apply, and what an AI seat costs in billable time.
verdict: Most firms with 20+ lawyers already use or pilot AI,[^1] but many still have no written AI policy.[^4]
Start with discovery review. It was about 73% of electronic-discovery production cost,[^5] and courts have accepted AI-assisted review since 2012.[^6]
A lawyer still checks every citation and signs.[^10] Courts have flagged AI-invented citations in hundreds of decisions involving lawyers.[^7]
Lawyers must keep client data in access-restricted tools that don't train on it, per ABA guidance[^10] and California law.[^11]
AI seats cost little next to lawyer time: every published price we checked is under 90 billable minutes a month.[^13][^15]

summary: AI for law firms is software that reads, searches and drafts: discovery review, summaries, research and first drafts.[^3] What changes is where lawyer hours go: RAND found computer-assisted review could cut attorney review hours by about three-quarters.[^5] A lawyer still checks each citation and signs, as ABA Opinion 512 expects.[^10][^17]
humanRole: The signing lawyer checks every citation and owns the filing. In a 2025 Wyoming case against Walmart, two lawyers who only signed a brief with fake cases were fined $1,000 each.[^19][^20]

Managing partners set the AI policy and training, as ABA Opinion 512 and California's 2026 guidance expect.[^10][^21] A federal court fined a supervising lawyer $1,001 in 2026 for not supervising a junior colleague's AI brief.[^22]
The litigation support or e-discovery lead checks AI document review by sampling. Courts expect a review process with quality-control testing.[^6][^23]

The risk partner or general counsel reads vendor terms before client data goes in. The client gives informed consent before self-learning tools see their data, and boilerplate doesn't count.[^10][^12]

ranked.name: Document review in discovery
ranked.why: Review was about 73% of e-discovery production cost in RAND's study of 57 large cases.[^5] Courts have accepted technology-assisted review (TAR) since 2012, if you check its quality by sampling.[^6][^24]
ranked.payoff: Reviewer hours per 1,000 documents, and the share of relevant documents found in a checked sample.

ranked.name: Summaries of depositions, productions and medical records
ranked.why: Among lawyers who use generative AI, 73% use it to summarise documents.[^3] Vendors claim big savings, such as EvenUp's 9+ hours per case; those are their own figures.[^25][^26]
ranked.payoff: Paralegal and associate hours per summary, and days to turnaround.

ranked.name: First-pass legal research and memos
ranked.why: Research is the top legal AI use, at 80% of users.[^3] It pays only with a cite-check: paid legal research tools still invented answers 17% to 33% of the time.[^18]
ranked.payoff: Hours to a first usable memo, and citation errors caught per memo.

ranked.name: Drafting letters and contracts
ranked.why: Among legal AI users, 55% draft correspondence with it and 49% draft contracts.[^3] A lawyer edits and sends every draft.[^10]

ranked.name: Time capture and billing prep
ranked.why: The average lawyer captured about 3 billable hours in an 8-hour day in 2025.[^27] Clio says firms on its AI tools log 6.5% more billable hours; that is the vendor's own data.[^28]
ranked.payoff: Billable hours captured per lawyer per day, and days from work done to invoice.

ranked.name: Intake and client updates
ranked.why: Of firms using AI, 65% say it helped them answer clients faster, per Clio's survey.[^29] Florida's ethics opinion says an intake chatbot must disclose it is AI, not a lawyer.[^30]
ranked.payoff: Hours to answer a new inquiry, and the share of inquiries that become clients.

ownData.title: What does an AI seat cost, in billable hours?
ownData.intro: Zavient checked the pricing pages of 18 AI tools law firms use, on 26 Nov 2026. We divided each seat price by $362 an hour, the average lawyer rate in billing data from Clio, a practice-management software vendor.[^13] The result is how much billable time a lawyer must free up each month to cover the seat.

rules.name: ABA Formal Opinion 512
rules.what: The baseline duties: understand the tool, check its output, protect client data and bill fairly.[^10][^46] Get informed consent before client data goes into self-learning tools.[^10] Persuasive in most states, not binding.[^10]

rules.name: FRCP 11 (Federal Rules of Civil Procedure) and state equivalents
rules.what: Signing a filing certifies you checked the law.[^20] Courts fine signers who didn't draft, too.[^19] The Fifth Circuit says the same sanctions rules apply to AI.[^47]

rules.name: California SB 574
rules.what: No delegating the practice of law to AI, and no confidential data in tools without restricted access.[^11] Verify every citation and disclose AI use on court filings.[^11][^48]

rules.name: State Bar of California guidance (2026)
rules.what: Managing lawyers should set AI policies, including for agentic tools that act on their own.[^21] More autonomy means more supervision.[^21]

rules.name: New York courts, Part 161
rules.what: AI use is allowed and there is no general duty to disclose it.[^49] Some courts may make your signature certify no fabricated content.[^49]

rules.name: NYSBA ethics guidelines (New York State Bar)
rules.what: Assume consumer AI chats are neither confidential nor privileged.[^50] Don't bill hours AI saved.[^50]

rules.name: Florida Bar Opinion 24-1
rules.what: Get consent before third-party AI sees confidential data, and don't double-bill.[^30] Intake chatbots must say they are AI, not a lawyer.[^30]

rules.name: Texas Ethics Opinion 705
rules.what: Texas's advisory opinion on generative AI covers competence, confidentiality, checking output and fees.[^51]

rules.name: D.C. Bar Opinion 388
rules.what: Consider keeping AI chats on a matter in the client file.[^52]

rules.name: Judges' own AI rules
rules.what: Some courts require you to disclose AI use, such as Local Rule 7.2(f) in the Northern District of Texas.[^53] Check each judge's rules before you file.[^53]

watchOuts: Fake citations in filings: courts have flagged AI-invented citations in hundreds of decisions involving lawyers.[^7] Open every cited case in a primary source before you file.[^20]

Big firms aren't immune: an Alabama federal court disqualified three Butler Snow lawyers in 2025.[^8][^54] It released the firm, which had acted reasonably to prevent misuse, so write your policy down.[^8]

Co-counsel you didn't ask: in a 2025 case against State Farm, two firms paid $31,100 after one never asked whether co-counsel used AI.[^9] Ask co-counsel and staff, and put it in work-sharing terms.[^9][^22]

Client data in a consumer account: a New York federal court held a client's consumer AI chats were not privileged in 2026.[^12][^55] Use a business tier with written no-training and retention terms.[^41][^14]

Billing the hours AI saved: bill actual time, including review, but not time learning the tool.[^46][^50][^56] A quarter of firms already report fewer billable hours on some tasks, so consider flat fees there.[^57]
No baseline, so no proof: only 18% of professionals say their organization measures AI's return; record hours per task before a pilot.[^3][^4]

faq.q: Can our lawyers paste client documents into ChatGPT?
faq.a: Not into a consumer ChatGPT account; use a business or enterprise tier whose terms bar training and restrict access.[^10][^11][^12] Get informed consent before self-learning tools see client data.[^10]

faq.q: Do we have to tell clients we use AI?
faq.a: Not always: ABA 512 says tell clients when they ask, the engagement requires it, consent is needed, or AI affects fees or significant decisions.[^10] California courts will require disclosure on filings from 1 Jan 2027.[^11]

faq.q: Can we still bill hourly for work AI sped up?
faq.a: Yes, but bill the time actually spent, including review, not the time AI saved.[^46][^50] Don't bill time spent learning the tool.[^46]

faq.q: Is legal-specific AI more accurate than ChatGPT?
faq.a: Not on accuracy: legal tools and ChatGPT both scored near 80% in Vals' 2025 benchmark, though legal tools cited better sources.[^42][^43] Paid legal tools still invented answers 17% to 33% of the time in Stanford's study.[^18]

faq.q: How much does legal AI cost?
faq.a: Legal AI costs $20 to $25 a seat a month for general tools, and about $100 to $499 for legal tools that publish a price.[^14][^31][^16][^15] Many legal tools quote only.[^35][^36] For 50 lawyers billed yearly, that is $12,000 a year on Claude or ChatGPT, or $78,000 on MyCase Advanced.[^14][^31][^16]
No: from 2027, California bars delegating the practice of law to AI, and a lawyer must sign every filing.[^11][^20]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when the work is standard or the data isn't yours: case law research needs licensed databases, and e-discovery platforms have court acceptance.[^36][^24] Most enterprise AI is now bought: 76% of use cases in 2025.[^58] Bought tools succeeded about twice as often as internal builds in MIT's study.[^59][^60]
buyVsBuild.build: Build a light layer when your edge is your own precedents, playbooks and clause bank. General models matched legal tools on research accuracy in Vals' benchmark.[^42] California's access rule favours setups where the firm controls who sees client data.[^11][^14]

pickElse: Small discovery sets: use keyword search and manual review, or a pay-per-gigabyte platform such as Logikcull. Courts framed AI review for large data volumes.[^6][^38]
You need citable authority: use the AI inside your existing Westlaw or Lexis subscription before a general chatbot. Legal tools scored higher on authoritative sources.[^42][^36]
You already run Clio or MyCase: switch on the AI in your current plan first. MyCase Pro includes writing and document assistants.[^33][^16]
Personal injury demand letters at volume: a specialist such as EvenUp or Supio may beat a build. Their outcome numbers are their own claims.[^25][^26]

offer.heading: Which matters should AI touch first at your firm?
offer.body: Litigation matters with large discovery should touch AI first, starting with document review, then summaries of depositions and records. In 30 minutes, bring one practice area and leave with the first workflow to try, your states' added rules, and hours to measure before buying. It is free, and you talk to the person who does the work.

reviews.notes: Would skip: the proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 row (not in force, rarely relevant) made an 11-row rules table long on a phone; cut it. Wouldn't understand: 'e-discovery' and 'per GB'; defined e-discovery on first use and wrote out gigabyte. Kept the ranked list short (one 'why' and one 'payoff' line each) so it scans on a 390px screen.

Own-data column 'Lawyer minutes to cover it' didn't say per month; renamed to 'Billable minutes a month to cover it'. Payoff lines are already countable (hours per 1,000 documents, days to invoice), which is what I'd report up. No other change.

Missing my real worry: AI that saves time cuts hourly revenue. Added the Best Law Firms finding that a quarter of firms already bill fewer hours on some tasks, with flat fees as the fix, to the billing watch-out. Would distrust Clio's '6.5% more billable hours'; it is already labelled vendor data.

As managing partner / head of legal operations: the ABA 512 disclosure list dropped 'shapes a significant decision'; added it. Changed 'state twins' to 'state equivalents'. Removed an unsourced line that firms on Microsoft 'often start' with Copilot, and an unsourced claim about who ran the studies. Gave Harvey's description its sourced wording (research, drafting, Vault). Supervising-lawyer fine now says 'junior colleague', matching the source. 'Hallucinated' now glossed as 'made up'.

Steve wants the bill for a firm his size, not per-seat maths. Added the 50-lawyer yearly cost ($12,000 on Claude or ChatGPT, $78,000 on MyCase Advanced) to the cost FAQ. Offer body rewritten in his words: bring one practice area, leave with the first workflow, the state rules and the hours to measure; free, with the person who does the work. Price clarity is in the own-data table, so no other change.

answers.human-role: Lawyers keep the judgment and the signature: the signing lawyer checks every citation and owns the filing, and managing partners set the AI policy.[^19][^20][^10] The e-discovery lead samples AI document review, and the risk partner vets vendor terms before client data goes in.[^6][^23][^10]
answers.ranked: AI pays first in document review for discovery, which was about 73% of e-discovery production cost, and courts have accepted it since 2012.[^5][^6] Next come summaries of depositions and records, first-pass research with a cite-check, and drafting.[^3][^18]
answers.own-data: An AI seat costs 3 to 4 billable minutes a month on Claude or ChatGPT, and at most about 83 minutes for any legal tool with a published price.[^13][^14][^31][^15] Those figures assume $362 an hour, Clio's average lawyer rate.[^13]
answers.table-1: Law firms use general assistants (Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft 365 Copilot), legal research tools (Lexis+ with Protégé, Westlaw, Harvey), and e-discovery and practice-management platforms.[^14][^31][^32][^36][^18][^35] ChatGPT is the tool lawyers use or consider most, at 52.1% in the ABA's 2024 survey.[^45]
answers.table-2: Independent studies find AI beats lawyers on legal research accuracy, about 80% against 71%, yet paid legal research tools still invent answers 17% to 33% of the time.[^43][^42][^18] Document review, where AI review helps, was about 73% of e-discovery cost in RAND's study.[^5]
answers.table-3: Most firms with 20 or more lawyers use AI: 87% of Texas firms with 25+ attorneys, and 64% of firms with 20+ lawyers in a 5,800-firm survey.[^2][^1] Smaller firms lag: 64% of smaller Texas firms use it.[^2]
answers.rules: ABA Formal Opinion 512 sets the baseline duties and Rule 11 makes every signer check the law; California, New York, Florida, Texas and D.C. add their own.[^10][^20][^11][^49][^30][^51][^52] Some judges also require you to disclose AI use, so check each court's rules before you file.[^53]
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI goes wrong for law firms through fake citations in filings, client data in consumer accounts, unchecked co-counsel, and billing hours AI saved.[^7][^12][^9][^50] Courts have flagged AI-invented citations in hundreds of decisions involving lawyers.[^7]
answers.faq: Lawyers ask about client data, telling clients, billing, accuracy, cost and jobs. The short answers: use business tiers only, disclose when ABA 512 calls for it, bill actual time, and check every citation.[^10][^46][^18]
answers.buy-or-build: Buy for standard work like case law research and e-discovery, and build only a light layer on your own precedents, playbooks and clause bank.[^36][^24][^42] Bought tools succeeded about twice as often as internal builds in MIT's study.[^59][^60]
answers.something-else: Pick keyword search for small discovery sets, the AI already in your Westlaw, Lexis, Clio or MyCase plan, or a specialist like EvenUp for injury demand letters.[^6][^38][^36][^16][^25]
